title: Teach it right the first time
statement: Teach a concept correctly when it first comes up, never skipping it as obvious, and at once state its key constraint and what it is not, with a counterexample.
detail: The science misconception cards rate first introductions as the riskiest points: in the gap before particles are explained, students build macroscopic mental models that become the default, and the highest risk for bonding is the moment it is first taught. Their synthesis asks for conservation to be stated together with the concept it governs, and for negative definitions, things students must be told are not true, to be taught explicitly; the chemistry card found no standards framework that gives the one for particles, and the science review workbook adds it as required at Grade 3. The biology card pairs its negative definition with a counterexample, and the physics card forbids skipping a law of motion because it seems obvious, since it is the one everyday experience contradicts most.

evidence.quote: Do NOT skip the first law because it "seems obvious." It is the LEAST obvious law and the one most contradicted by everyday experience.
a true, positively-stated contrast that draws the concept's edge ("a cell is alive; an atom is a smaller, non-living piece")
It is NOT a negation of the student misconception and NOT a "what X is NOT" line.
The key cross-cutting insight: energy conservation must be taught at the SAME TIME energy is introduced (as the Franklin Standards do at grade 3), not as a later addition.
